oil.summary: WTI and Brent surged 4.34% and 4.22% respectively on Monday, with Brent touching $79.23 and pressing toward the $80 handle, as the Strait of Hormuz crisis entered a new and more dangerous phase. Iran closed the strait following a third consecutive weekend of U.S. military strikes, with the IRGC warning of further oil and gas disruptions should U.S. interference continue. Oil and LNG tankers are once again going dark on transponders through the passage. Separately, Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery, while a White House-backed sanctions bill threatens 500% tariffs on Chinese and Indian buyers of Russian crude. Nigerian production hitting a six-year high provides a partial offset. The notable exception is RBOB gasoline, which fell 2.65% on the day, suggesting some demand-side softness even as crude rallied hard on geopolitical risk premia.
drivers: Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz after a third weekend of U.S. strikes triggers acute supply-disruption fears, lifting WTI +4.34% and Brent +4.22%
Compounding supply risk: Ukraine struck a Russian refinery and proposed U.S. secondary sanctions threaten 500% tariffs on buyers of Russian crude
Partial offsets—Nigeria's six-year-high output and Iranian barrels stuck at sea as Chinese teapots pivot away—cap the upside; RBOB's -2.65% drop signals demand-side caution

gas.summary: The Atlantic gas complex is sharply bifurcated today. TTF rocketed 6.43% to €51.785/MWh, extending a weekly gain now exceeding 17%, as the Hormuz escalation directly threatens LNG transit routes from the Gulf. Iran's reported strikes against five Gulf countries hosting U.S. forces add a broader regional dimension to the supply threat. Tankers going dark in the strait amplify the risk premium. Against this backdrop, the EU is scrambling to secure alternatives, with Russian Yamal LNG imports hitting a record 9.97 million metric tons ahead of the 2027 ban—a politically uncomfortable but commercially rational hedge. Henry Hub, insulated from Middle East logistics, slid 1.90% to $2.884/MMBtu and is off more than 11% on the week, reflecting abundant domestic supply and a structurally different market dynamic.
drivers: Hormuz closure and LNG tanker transponder blackouts drive TTF +6.43% on the day and +17.34% on the week as European spot markets price acute supply disruption risk
Iran striking five Gulf nations hosting U.S. forces widens the regional threat perimeter, putting Gulf LNG export infrastructure at risk
Henry Hub continues to diverge sharply, down 1.90% on the day and -11.12% on the week, reflecting domestic U.S. supply insulation from Middle East events

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs edged up just 0.59% to $75.50, a muted session relative to the volatility seen in the underlying energy complex, though the one-month trend remains modestly positive at +3.35%. The key power-sector story today is France's forced curtailment of 6.4 GW of nuclear capacity due to a heatwave raising river temperatures and limiting cooling water availability—precisely the wrong moment as gas-fired backup becomes more expensive with TTF at €51.785/MWh and rising. On the structural side, Masdar announced $5.1 billion in financing for the world's largest solar-and-battery round-the-clock renewable project, a notable milestone. However, utility-scale solar costs have risen 18% to $40–$98/MWh due to tariffs, capital costs, and supply chain pressure. The Energy Institute's 2026 Statistical Review confirmed global emissions hit yet another record high despite the clean energy expansion.
drivers: France cuts 6.4 GW of nuclear output due to heatwave-driven river temperature constraints, tightening European power balances as gas backup costs surge with TTF at multi-month highs
EU EUA carbon price adds only 0.59% despite the broader energy volatility, suggesting the market is watching macro risk rather than pricing immediate carbon demand shifts
Structural tensions persist: Masdar's $5.1bn gigascale solar-and-battery financing signals clean energy momentum, but global emissions hit a fresh record and utility-scale solar costs are up 18%
